nodes.label: Executive summary
nodes.one_line: Compress the whole proposal into the one-page summary reviewers actually read first, hitting every scoring criterion in miniature.
know_what: Executive summary — the one-page distillation placed first in the proposal that program officers and panelists read before the narrative
First-read position — reviewers skim the summary first and carry its impression into the narrative, so it must carry the whole argument
Review-criteria mirroring — the convention of hitting every scoring criterion in miniature, in the criteria's own order
Stand-alone test — the summary must make sense to someone who reads nothing else in the packet
The ask in numbers — amount, duration, and what the money funds, stated explicitly instead of left for the budget
One-page rule — most foundations cap the summary at one page; federal project-summary fields have their own word counts that must be checked per NOFO
Forward references — phrases like 'as detailed in the approach section' that spend words without earning credibility
know_how: Write the summary after the narrative is complete, then place it first in the document
Open with the problem and the project in one sentence each, never with the organization's history
Mirror the review criteria in order, one sentence per criterion, using the funder's own vocabulary
State the ask — dollar amount, duration, and what it buys — in the first half of the page
Tighten to the funder's stated page or word limit, cutting adjectives before cutting claims
Run the stand-alone test: hand the summary alone to a reader and have them restate the project
habits: Drafting the summary last but checking it first on every revision pass
Re-reading the summary after every narrative change so the two cannot drift apart
Keeping a boilerplate one-liner for the organization's mission and track record to reuse across funders
Treating 'the reviewer will see it in the narrative' as a reason to cut, not to pad
Checking the funder's summary-field spec (word count, plain text, portal box) before writing
nodes.checkpoint: Write a one-page executive summary, from a finished narrative, in which a cold reader can restate the problem, the approach, the outcomes, and the dollar ask, with every review criterion hit in miniature.
nodes.common_failure: Writing the summary first and letting the narrative drift from it, so the document contradicts its own front page; or padding it past one page — reviewers who read the summary first carry its sloppiness into the rest of the score.
sources: Karsh & Fox, The Only Grant-Writing Book You'll Ever Need
Carlson & O'Neal-McElrath, Winning Grants Step by Step

nodes.label: Project abstract
nodes.one_line: Write the 250-word abstract that must stand alone in the funder's portal and win the skim.
know_what: Abstract — the 200-250 word summary that lives in the funder's portal or application form, often the only part read by non-panel staff and the part databases index
250-word convention — most portals and NOFOs cap the abstract at 200-250 words; the cap is a hard field limit, not a suggestion
Plain-text constraint — portal abstract fields usually strip formatting, so bold, bullets, and tables are lost on paste
Stand-alone unit — the abstract is read and searched detached from the proposal it summarizes
Structured abstract — the background-objectives-methods-expected-results shape some federal programs mandate
Keyword indexing — agencies and databases surface proposals by abstract terms, so the words you choose are searchable metadata
Abstract vs executive summary — the abstract is a portal field; the executive summary is a document section; they are written separately even where they overlap
know_how: Read the NOFO or portal spec first: exact word count, plain-text requirement, and any mandated structure
Draft from the specific aims or SMART objectives, mirroring their order and language
Front-load the first 30 words with population, intervention, and expected outcome
Write the abstract last, once the narrative is final, so every claim in it exists in the full text
Count words against the field limit and cut to about 95% of the cap rather than trusting truncation
Paste the final text into the portal field and re-check for characters the form strips, such as quotes and ampersands
Run the stand-alone test: a reader who sees only the abstract can state what is being done, for whom, and with what expected result
habits: Writing the abstract after the narrative is frozen, never before
Keeping a sentence template — population, problem, approach, outcome, ask — so abstracts stay skimmable
Checking every abstract against the NOFO's stated word limit before pasting
Re-reading the abstract in the portal preview, not just in the word processor
Choosing the same field terms the funder uses, since the abstract is searchable metadata
nodes.checkpoint: Write a 250-word abstract under the funder's stated limit that survives detachment — a reader who sees only the abstract can state the population, the approach, the expected outcome, and the ask.
nodes.common_failure: Pasting the executive summary into the abstract field and blowing the word limit, or writing the abstract first and letting the narrative drift — either way the portal text and the proposal disagree at the point of first skim.
sources: Karsh & Fox, The Only Grant-Writing Book You'll Ever Need

nodes.label: Attachment pack
nodes.one_line: Assemble the supporting documents — org budget, bios, letters of support, financials — that reviewers check for capacity and credibility.
know_what: Required attachments — the funder's checklist: biosketches or resumes, org budget, board list, IRS determination letter, audited financials, letters of support
Biosketch conventions — NIH-style biosketch or the funder's resume format, naming the person's role on this project and its effort percent, not a general CV
Letters of support — third-party letters that name the writer, the organization, and the specific commitment, not generic praise
Org budget vs project budget — the full organizational budget (all revenue and expenses) that reviewers read for capacity, distinct from the project budget
Audited or reviewed financials — the prior year's statements that prove the organization can actually handle the money
IRS determination letter — the 501(c)(3) letter proving charitable status; foundations routinely require a current copy
Portal constraints — per-file size limits (commonly 50MB on Grants.gov), allowed file formats, and file-naming rules
know_how: Copy the funder's attachment checklist into a tracking sheet and mark each item owned and done before submission week
Prepare biosketches that tie each person to this project's role and effort, not a generic CV dump
Solicit letters of support early with a template that names the writer, the relationship, and the specific commitment
Convert every document to the portal's required format (usually PDF) and rename per the funder's naming convention
Verify file sizes and formats against the portal limits before submission, not after the upload fails
Cross-check names, titles, and effort in the attachments against the narrative so the personnel story agrees everywhere
Keep a master folder of evergreen attachments (determination letter, org chart, board list) with current dates and versions
habits: Building the attachment pack in parallel with the narrative, never the night before submission
Requesting letters of support at least two weeks before the deadline
Re-reading every attachment for stale dates and facts before each new submission
Keeping a per-funder attachment checklist so nothing is assumed from a prior application
Verifying each PDF opens and renders correctly before uploading
nodes.checkpoint: Produce a complete attachment pack matching the funder's checklist — every required document present, correctly named, under every portal size limit, and consistent with the narrative's personnel and budget.
nodes.common_failure: Treating attachments as afterthoughts: generic form letters of support that name no commitment, org budgets two years out of date, or an expired determination letter — reviewers read the pack as the capacity evidence, and a mismatch kills credibility.
sources: Carlson & O'Neal-McElrath, Winning Grants Step by Step

nodes.label: Personnel & fringe
nodes.one_line: Price staff time with real salaries and fringe rates, allocating effort across funded and unfunded time so the budget survives scrutiny.
know_what: Personnel line — salaries and wages for named or to-be-hired staff, usually the largest line in a project budget
Percent effort — the fraction of a person's time charged to the grant, shown as a percentage or FTE (e.g., 25% = 0.25 FTE) with the resulting dollar amount
Fringe rate — the employer-side costs added to salary: payroll taxes, health insurance, retirement; typically 25-40% of salary depending on the employer
Funded vs unfunded time — the split of a person's effort between grant-supported and other work, which reviewers check for realism
Salary cap — the ceiling on grant-charged salary, e.g., the NIH cap tied to Executive Level II (about $231,000 in 2025) that resets each January
Payroll-based pricing — pricing from the actual payroll amount or hiring range, not a round guess, so the budget matches what finance will actually pay
New-hire pricing — quoting a to-be-hired salary at the hiring step or grade HR will use, with the start date in the right budget year
know_how: Price each person from the actual payroll or the hiring range, then add the fringe rate on top
Show effort as a percentage or FTE per person with the resulting dollars, so the math is checkable
Allocate effort across funded and unfunded time — a person at 50% grant, 50% other — so the budget never implies more than 1.0 FTE
Apply the fringe rate as a percentage of salary in the same period the payroll uses
Check each salary against any funder cap (e.g., the NIH salary cap) and cap the charged amount at it
Reconcile personnel totals to the payroll report or an HR letter so the numbers survive an audit
Price future years with the cost-of-living increment the organization actually grants, not a uniform guess
habits: Pricing personnel from payroll, never from 'what we wish we could pay'
Questioning any line where effort and salary imply more than 1.0 FTE
Keeping the organization's current fringe rate documented and re-checking it each budget cycle
Checking salary caps and effort rules for every new federal program before pricing staff
Running the personnel page past the person whose time it charges
nodes.checkpoint: Produce a personnel section where each named or to-be-hired role shows salary, fringe rate and amount, and percent effort that sums to a realistic allocation, with every number traceable to payroll or HR.
nodes.common_failure: Pricing staff at round-number salaries with no fringe, or charging one person at 100% effort across three grants — the math fails an auditor and the reviewer reads the staffing story as fantasy.

nodes.label: Allowable costs
nodes.one_line: Check every line against federal cost principles and the funder's restrictions so nothing unallowable or disqualifying is requested.
know_what: Allowable cost — a cost that passes 2 CFR 200.403: necessary, reasonable, allocable, treated consistently, and within the funder's limitations
2 CFR 200 (Uniform Guidance) — the federal cost principles defining allowable, allocable, and reasonable for every federal award
Unallowable categories — 2 CFR 200.438 entertainment (tickets, social activities, alcohol), 200.450 lobbying, 200.442 fundraising, 200.445 goods or services for personal use
Allocability — a cost is allocable when it benefits the award in proportion to its share, the test that governs shared staff, rent, and utilities
Reasonable-person test — whether a prudent person would pay this price for this good or service in this market
Prior approval — 2 CFR 200.407 items that need the funder's written consent before they can be charged, such as certain equipment or participant support
Funder restrictions — foundation and corporate exclusions (no capital campaigns, no regranting, no religious activity) that sit on top of federal rules
Equipment threshold — the useful-life-plus-cost definition (commonly $5,000) that moves an item from supplies into tracked equipment
know_how: Run every proposed line through the 200.403 test — necessary, reasonable, allocable, consistent, within limitations — before it reaches the budget
Check each category against the unallowable list — entertainment, lobbying, fundraising, alcohol — early, not after review
Classify shared costs (rent, utilities, admin staff) as direct or indirect once, and treat them the same way every year
Flag anything needing prior approval under 200.407 and request the funder's written consent in the budget justification
Read the funder's own exclusion list and line-check the draft budget against it
Keep a written rationale for each borderline line — an auditor will ask why it was allowed
Recheck the organization's capitalization policy when an item crosses the equipment threshold
habits: Keeping the 2 CFR 200 unallowable list open while building any federal budget
Questioning every line with 'would this survive an auditor?' before it ships
Noting the funder's exclusions on the budget cover sheet so they are visible at review
Documenting borderline decisions in writing the same week, not after the audit letter arrives
Re-reading the NOFO's cost section for program-specific restrictions, such as no food or no construction
nodes.checkpoint: Produce a line-checked budget where every line passes the 200.403 test, nothing on the funder's exclusion list is requested, and the borderline calls are documented in writing.
nodes.common_failure: Assuming a cost is allowable because the program needs it — an entertainment-heavy conference line or a lobbying-adjacent activity gets requested, and the award gets flagged or the proposal rejected for asking.
sources: NIH Grants Policy Statement — cost considerations
Karsh & Fox, The Only Grant-Writing Book You'll Ever Need

nodes.label: Indirect cost rates
nodes.one_line: Calculate indirect costs using your negotiated rate, the funder's cap, or the 10% de minimis rate, and present them so they don't get cut.
know_what: Indirect costs (F&A) — the organization's shared overhead — facilities, administration, finance, HR, IT — recovered as a percentage of a cost base
Negotiated indirect cost rate agreement (NICRA) — the rate your cognizant agency (typically HHS for nonprofits) approved after a rate negotiation
10% de minimis rate — 2 CFR 200.414(f): entities that have never held a negotiated rate may claim a flat 10% of modified total direct costs with no negotiation and no documentation
Modified total direct cost (MTDC) base — direct costs minus equipment, capital expenditures, participant support, rental costs, and the portion of each subaward over $25,000
Funder caps — many foundations cap indirect at 10-15% of direct costs, and some federal programs cap F&A (e.g., NIH's 8% cap on foreign components)
Rate basis — whether the rate applies to the full direct base or the MTDC base changes the dollars materially, so the base must match the agreement
Cognizant agency — the federal agency that negotiates and issues your NICRA, which you approach for rate changes and renegotiation
know_how: Find your rate in order: check for a current NICRA first; only if none exists and none ever has, elect the 10% de minimis
Identify the base the funder wants — MTDC vs total direct costs — and compute the indirect line on that base
Exclude from the MTDC base: equipment, capital expenditures, participant support, rental costs, and each subaward's amount over $25,000
Apply a funder's cap (e.g., 10-15%) when it is lower than your NICRA, and show the capped calculation
Present the rate and its base explicitly: '10% de minimis on MTDC' rather than a bare indirect number
Attach the NICRA, or the de minimis election statement, to federal budget submissions
Re-negotiate the NICRA on its cycle and re-check it before each year's applications
habits: Checking for a NICRA before defaulting to de minimis — the de minimis is for never-negotiated entities only
Stating the rate and its base on every budget so the reviewer never has to guess
Treating a funder's 'indirects not allowed' line as a negotiation point, not a final word
Keeping the NICRA and the de minimis election in the attachment master folder, current
Recomputing the indirect line whenever the direct base changes, so the two never disagree

know_why.claim: Claim the full negotiated indirect rate on every award that allows it — a lower rate is donated overhead.
know_why.because: the negotiated rate is the federal government's own determination of your real infrastructure cost, and accepting a funder's cap or the de minimis permanently underfunds the finance, HR, and IT that the grant itself depends on.
know_why.disputed_by: small-nonprofit grant writers who accept a funder's cap or the 10% de minimis to look lean, arguing that a lower indirect line improves competitiveness where reviewers read overhead as bloat and where the rate-negotiation burden is not worth the recovery.
know_why.source: 2 CFR 200.414(c)-(f); NIH foreign-component F&A cap (NOT-OD-11-042); practitioner debate in The Grantsmanship Center Magazine

nodes.checkpoint: Produce an indirect cost line that names the rate, its basis (NICRA, funder cap, or 10% de minimis), and the base it applies to, with the calculation shown and any cap applied.
nodes.common_failure: Leaving indirect costs out entirely to look lean and losing real overhead recovery, or applying a NICRA rate to the wrong base (total direct costs instead of MTDC) and overstating the line — either way the budget misrepresents the organization's real costs.
sources: HHS Cost Allocation Services — indirect cost rate negotiation

nodes.label: Match & cost share
nodes.one_line: Identify a required match or cost share and document how it will be met — cash, in-kind, or third-party — before it becomes a compliance problem.
know_what: Match (cost share) — the portion of project costs the applicant must fund from its own or third-party sources, expressed as a percentage or ratio
Cash match — actual dollars from the applicant or a third party, governed by the same cost principles as the requested funds
In-kind match — donated goods, services, or volunteer time valued at fair market value and documented
Third-party match — contributions from partners, funders, or donors that count toward the requirement with a written commitment
2 CFR 200.306 — the federal match rules: verifiable from the organization's records, not funded by another federal award, necessary, reasonable, and allowable
Match ratios in the wild — e.g., JAG's 25% (cash or in-kind), FEMA's 25% non-federal share on hazard mitigation, PCORI's 50% of total project cost
Match documentation — time-and-effort logs for donated staff time, donor letters for cash pledges, and valuation worksheets for donated goods
know_how: Read the NOFO or guidelines for the exact ratio, the base it applies to (total project cost vs requested funds), and whether cash, in-kind, or both qualify
Inventory real match capacity before deciding to pursue: volunteer hours, donated space, partner contributions, and existing cash
Choose cash or in-kind according to what the funder allows and what the organization can actually document
Secure third-party match with written commitments before submission, never after the award
Valuate in-kind contributions at fair market value and keep the valuation worksheet with the match records
Exclude anything paid by another federal award from the match — 200.306 forbids double-counting
Budget the match line explicitly on the same budget form so reviewers see the match is planned, not hoped for
habits: Checking the match ratio before the go/no-go fit decision, not after the draft is written
Keeping a running inventory of in-kind capacity (volunteer hours, donated space) so the match is real, not invented
Documenting match at the time it happens — time sheets and commitment letters, not reconstructed at audit
Flagging any match funded from another federal source as a compliance error, immediately
Treating 'we'll find the match later' as a reason to pass on the opportunity

know_why.claim: Match-heavy awards are worth chasing — the required match multiplies scarce cash and signals commitment that scores.
know_why.because: in programs like PCORI (50% of total project cost) and JAG (25%), the match is mandatory and often scored, and an organization with real in-kind capacity can convert volunteer hours and donated space into leverage it could never raise in cash.
know_why.disputed_by: program-integrity-minded grant managers who argue the match distorts the program — the design gets shaped around what is matchable rather than what is needed, and misvalued or undocumented match becomes an audit finding and a repayment at closeout.
know_why.source: 2 CFR 200.306; PCORI funding announcements (50% match); DOJ JAG match guidance; practitioner debate in The Grantsmanship Center Magazine

nodes.checkpoint: Given a NOFO with a match requirement, produce a match plan naming the ratio, the base, the cash and in-kind sources, the valuation method, and the documentation trail, all compliant with 200.306.
nodes.common_failure: Committing to a match the organization cannot document — counting hoped-for volunteer hours or a partner's verbal pledge — then failing the award's match verification at closeout, which can turn the grant into a repayment.

nodes.label: Multi-year budget
nodes.one_line: Lay out a multi-year budget with annual escalation and changing match requirements so the full award period is coherent.
know_what: Multi-year budget — a budget with a column per budget period (usually a year) plus a total column, spanning the full project period
Annual escalation — the 3-5% per-year increase applied to salaries, supplies, and contracted costs for inflation and steps
SF424A — the federal multi-year budget summary form with object-class categories across budget-period columns
Budget period vs project period — the funded year(s) vs the full award term; the multi-year budget covers the project period
Step increases — the annual salary step or cost-of-living bump the organization actually grants, which escalation must mirror rather than replace
Changing match by year — requirements that ramp up or phase out across budget periods (e.g., 25% in year one, 50% in year two) shown explicitly
Ramp-down — the final year's reduction in activities and costs as the project winds toward sustainability or continuation funding
Carryover — unspent funds the funder may allow into the next budget period, which affects how conservatively each year is priced
know_how: Set the project period and list every budget period with its start and end dates before pricing anything
Apply annual escalation to salary and supply lines at the organization's real increment, typically 3-5%
Add a column per year plus a total column, with cross-year formulas so no year can drift silently
Lay out the match year by year if the requirement changes, and show the cumulative total against the requirement
Price new hires in the year they start and step existing staff annually, rather than flat-lining headcount
Recompute the indirect line per year, since the base grows with escalation
Ramp down the final year's activities to a sustainable level instead of ending at full speed
Reconcile the multi-year total to the funder's form (e.g., SF424A sections) before submission
habits: Escalating from real payroll increments, not a universal 5% guess
Checking the funder's multi-year template before building columns, so the form and the spreadsheet agree
Reviewing the multi-year budget against the narrative's year-by-year activity plan
Flagging any year where the match or the indirect rate changes, with the reason on the sheet
Freezing prior-year columns once submitted, so revisions never ripple backwards
nodes.checkpoint: Produce a multi-year budget with a column per budget period, annual escalation applied consistently, match and indirect recomputed per year, and a grand total that reconciles to the funder's form.
nodes.common_failure: Copying year one's budget into later years unchanged — no escalation, no step increases, no ramp-down — so the out-years are fiction, or applying escalation to fixed costs like rent and equipment that do not inflate.
sources: 2 CFR 200.308 (revision of budget and program plans)
Carlson & O'Neal-McElrath, Winning Grants Step by Step
